Should luck decide how much we blame? Picture two drivers who both text while driving. One crosses an empty road and gets home; the other hits a child who steps into the street. Both chose the same risk; only chance made the difference. 

Philosophers call this moral luck: we judge people by results we didn’t control as well as by intentions we did. Strict fairness—the control principle—says that blame should track only what was within someone’s voluntary power. But legal systems and everyday reactions routinely punish actual harm more than failed attempts, because societies must manage real dangers, deter carelessness and respond to victims.

That practical defence helps explain why outcome-based judgement survives: it’s a regulatory tool, not a metaphysical ledger of souls. Still, it leaves a hard worry. If severity hinges on a roll of the dice, can we really call the system fair? 

Is it possible to preserve public accountability without making punishment depend on mere luck?

Should luck decide how much we blame? That tension cuts straight to how we talk about fairness and responsibility. Imagine two people who do the same reckless thing—texting while driving through a residential street. One drifts into an empty lane and gets home; the other hits a child who steps off the kerb at exactly the wrong moment. From the standpoint of intention and voluntary control, the two agents are indistinguishable. Yet we punish and condemn them very differently.

Philosophers call this problem moral luck. The control principle—our intuitive rule that people should be judged only for what lies within their voluntary power—implies that judging someone more harshly because circumstances happened to be worse is unfair. But legal systems and everyday practices routinely track outcomes as well as intent. Michael Moore’s legal theory and other pragmatic accounts treat punishment partly as a tool for managing risk, deterring dangerous conduct and responding to actualised harm. In this view, outcome-based distinctions are not accidental mistakes but features of institutions designed to keep people safe.

This pragmatic explanation explains why law often punishes completed harms more severely than identical attempts. Yet it does not dissolve the philosophical misgiving: if the difference between a light reprimand and severe condemnation can rest on whether a bystander moved a fraction of a second, then the link between desert and luck seems arbitrary. That arbitrariness admits a real moral cost, even if it performs regulatory work.

So where does that leave us? If our institutions must incorporate some arbitrariness to function, how should we redesign accountability so that it minimises the unfair burdens of constitutive and circumstantial luck without undermining deterrence and victim recognition?
